plainEnglish.summary: Every piece of non-text content shown to users has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose. Controls and inputs need a name that describes their purpose. Time-based media, tests that would be invalid in text, and content meant to create a specific sensory experience only need a text alternative that identifies them. A CAPTCHA needs a text alternative describing its purpose and a version that uses a different sense. Content that is pure decoration, used only for visual formatting, or not presented to users must be implemented so assistive technology can ignore it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Alt text can be present and equivalent yet still tiring to use, for example when it repeats the caption beside it or runs to a paragraph.

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded audio-only content has a text alternative that presents equivalent information (an "alternative for time-based media"). Prerecorded video-only content has either that text alternative or an audio track with equivalent information. Media that is itself an alternative for text, and clearly labeled as such, is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A transcript that technically exists but sits on another page, or is only linked from a footer, is easy to miss. Users who need it may never find it.

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded audio in synchronized media (video with sound) has captions. By definition, captions cover both speech and the non-speech audio needed to understand the content. Media that is a clearly labeled alternative for text is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Complete captions can still be hard to follow when they are split mid-phrase, cover on-screen text, or can't be resized.

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded video with sound has either a full text alternative for time-based media or audio description of the video. Media that is a clearly labeled alternative for text is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Meeting Level A with a text document means blind users leave the video to read instead of experiencing it with everyone else.

plainEnglish.summary: Live audio in synchronized media, such as a live-streamed event with video, has captions.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Complete live captions that lag well behind the speaker are hard to follow alongside the video.

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded video in synchronized media has audio description: narration added to describe important visual details that can't be understood from the main soundtrack alone.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Description squeezed into short pauses can leave out context. A separate described version is often hard to find, or lags behind updates to the main video.

plainEnglish.summary: Information, structure and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined, or are available in text. If something looks like a heading, list, table or group, that structure has to be available to software too.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A page can convey its structure with the bare minimum of semantics and still be slow to navigate. Without landmarks or a sensible heading outline, screen reader users have fewer ways to jump around.

plainEnglish.summary: When the order of content affects its meaning, a correct reading order can be programmatically determined.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: CSS that reorders content visually (flex order, grid placement) can still pass, yet keyboard and screen magnifier users see focus and reading jump around the screen.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft addresses reading sequence.

plainEnglish.summary: Instructions for understanding and operating content don't rely solely on sensory characteristics such as shape, color, size, visual location, orientation or sound.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Instructions that lead with position ("in the panel on the right") still slow down people who can't see the layout, or who see a reflowed version of it.

plainEnglish.summary: Content doesn't restrict its view and operation to a single display orientation (portrait or landscape) unless a specific orientation is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Content that technically rotates can still be awkward. In landscape on a phone, fixed headers and footers can leave only a sliver of usable space.

plainEnglish.summary: Input fields collecting information about the user have a programmatically determinable purpose, when the field's purpose is one listed in WCAG's Input Purposes section and the technology supports it. (In HTML, W3C's sufficient technique is the autocomplete attribute; techniques are informative.)
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Correct autocomplete values don't help if scripts or browser workarounds stop autofill from working. People with motor or memory impairments are left retyping their details.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft requires identifying input purpose. Automated entry allowed covers not blocking autofill or paste.

plainEnglish.summary: Color is not the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A second cue that meets 3:1 but is small, such as a small icon beside a red error message, is still easy for color-blind users to miss.

plainEnglish.summary: If audio plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, there is either a way to pause or stop it, or a way to control its volume separately from the system volume. Under WCAG's non-interference requirement this applies to everything on the page, even content not relied on to meet other criteria.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A pause button at the bottom of the page is hard to find for screen reader users, whose speech is drowned out by the audio while they look for it.

plainEnglish.summary: Text and images of text have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Large-scale text (at least 18pt, or 14pt bold) needs 3:1. Text in inactive components, pure decoration, invisible text, text inside pictures with significant other visual content, and logos have no contrast requirement.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: 4.5:1 is a floor. Thin or small fonts at exactly 4.5:1 can still be hard to read for people with low vision, in glare, or on low-quality screens.

wcag3Mapping.note: The draft's contrast measure is still to be determined.

plainEnglish.summary: Apart from captions and images of text, text can be resized up to 200 percent without assistive technology and without loss of content or functionality.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Many people enlarge only the text, through browser or OS font settings rather than zoom. Layouts with fixed heights can clip that text even when they pass with page zoom.

plainEnglish.summary: If the technology can produce the visual presentation, real text is used instead of images of text. Exceptions: the image of text can be visually customized (font, size, color and background can be set), or a particular presentation is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Text baked into banners and social cards can't be resized, recolored or reflowed, and blurs when magnified.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft restricts images of text.

plainEnglish.summary: Content can be presented without losing information or functionality, and without scrolling in two directions, at a width of 320 CSS pixels (for vertically scrolling content) or a height of 256 CSS pixels (for horizontally scrolling content). Parts of the content that need a two-dimensional layout for their use or meaning are exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A page can reflow while hiding key actions behind menus, or by covering much of the small viewport with sticky headers. People using 400% zoom then see very little content at once.

plainEnglish.summary: These have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors: the visual information needed to identify user interface components and their states (except inactive components, and components whose appearance is set by the browser and not modified by the author), and the parts of graphics needed to understand the content (unless a particular presentation is essential).
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A state change that meets 3:1 but is shown only by a thin border change is easy to miss.

plainEnglish.summary: In content built with markup languages, nothing is lost and nothing stops working when a user sets line height to 1.5 times the font size, spacing after paragraphs to 2 times, letter spacing to 0.12 times and word spacing to 0.16 times, changing no other style. Languages and scripts that don't use one of these properties are exempt for that property.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Layouts can survive the test values exactly but break with slightly larger user settings, or with fonts swapped in for dyslexia.

plainEnglish.summary: When hover or keyboard focus makes extra content appear (such as a custom tooltip or submenu): it can be dismissed without moving the pointer or focus, unless it shows an input error or doesn't cover other content; if triggered by hover, the pointer can move onto it without it disappearing; and it stays visible until the trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid. Content whose presentation the browser controls, such as a title-attribute tooltip, is exempt.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Hover content can pass and still be awkward on touch screens, where there is no hover, and for magnifier users who lose it off-screen.

plainEnglish.summary: All functionality can be operated through a keyboard interface, without needing specific timing for individual keystrokes. The exception is functionality whose underlying function depends on the path of the user's movement, not just its endpoints (such as freehand drawing).
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Something can be keyboard-operable yet take dozens of Tab presses, or rely on key combinations nobody would guess.

plainEnglish.summary: If keyboard focus can move into a component, it can move out again using only the keyboard. If leaving needs more than unmodified arrow or Tab keys or another standard exit method, the user is told how. Under WCAG's non-interference requirement this applies to everything on the page.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A non-standard exit that is documented somewhere technically passes, but users rarely find the instructions.

plainEnglish.summary: If a keyboard shortcut uses only a letter, punctuation, number or symbol key, at least one of these is true: it can be turned off; it can be remapped to include a non-printable key such as Ctrl or Alt; or it only works while the relevant component has focus.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A setting to turn shortcuts off that is hard to find leaves speech-input users accidentally triggering actions until they discover it.

plainEnglish.summary: For each time limit the content sets, at least one is true: the user can turn it off before reaching it; adjust it to at least ten times the default; or is warned before it expires and given at least 20 seconds to extend it with a simple action, at least ten times. The limit is exempt if it's a required part of a real-time event with no possible alternative, if it's essential and extending it would invalidate the activity, or if it's longer than 20 hours.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Twenty seconds to respond to a warning is short for people using screen readers, switch access or speech input, especially if the warning doesn't take focus or isn't announced.

plainEnglish.summary: Moving, blinking or scrolling information that starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds and is shown alongside other content can be paused, stopped or hidden, unless the movement is essential. Auto-updating information that starts automatically and is shown alongside other content can be paused, stopped or hidden, or its update frequency controlled, unless essential. Under WCAG's non-interference requirement this applies to everything on the page.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A small pause button that is hard to find, or that resets when the page reloads, still passes. Motion can distract people with attention-related disabilities long before they find it.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers auto-updating content.

plainEnglish.summary: Nothing on the page flashes more than three times in any one second, or the flashing is below the general flash and red flash thresholds defined in WCAG. Under WCAG's non-interference requirement this applies to everything on the page.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The thresholds are approximations. Content near them can still affect some people with photosensitive epilepsy, or cause migraines.

plainEnglish.summary: A mechanism is available to bypass blocks of content that are repeated on multiple pages.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Headings and landmarks help screen reader users but do nothing for sighted keyboard users, who must still tab through the whole header.

wcag3Mapping.note: Focus relevant's test procedure asks for a way to skip groups of repeated interactive elements, such as site navigation.

plainEnglish.summary: Pages have titles that describe their topic or purpose.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Descriptive titles with the site name first get cut off in narrow browser tabs, so users can't tell tabs apart.

plainEnglish.summary: If a page can be navigated sequentially and the order affects meaning or operation, focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An order that preserves meaning can still jump around the screen, which disorients sighted keyboard and magnifier users.

plainEnglish.summary: The purpose of each link can be determined from its text alone, or from its text together with its programmatically determined context, except where the purpose would be ambiguous to everyone.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Screen reader users who browse a list of links hear "Read more" ten times with no context, even though each link passes.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers link purpose.

plainEnglish.summary: The headings and labels you provide describe their topic or purpose.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Headings that are accurate but vague ("Details", "More") pass, yet make scanning slow.

plainEnglish.summary: Any keyboard-operable interface has a mode of operation in which the keyboard focus indicator is visible.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A visible indicator, even one that meets 3:1, can be hard to spot if it's thin or close in style to the hover state.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft requires a visible focus indicator as such; the related provisions cover its contrast and the use of the browser default.

plainEnglish.summary: When a component receives keyboard focus, it is not entirely hidden by content the author created.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A focused field that is 90% hidden behind a sticky footer passes, but keyboard users can't see what they're typing into.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers focus being obscured.

plainEnglish.summary: For components whose label includes text or images of text, the accessible name contains the text that is shown visually.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: If the visible words sit in the middle of a longer name, some speech-input tools match less reliably.

plainEnglish.summary: Functionality that uses dragging can also be done with a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the browser provides the functionality and the author hasn't modified it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An alternative that takes many taps, or sits in an overflow menu, technically passes but is tiring for people with motor impairments.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when: a 24 CSS pixel circle centered on each smaller target doesn't overlap another target or another such circle; the same function is available through another control on the page that meets this criterion; the target is in a sentence or limited by the line height of surrounding text; the browser sets the size and the author hasn't changed it; or the presentation is essential or legally required.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: 24 by 24 is still small for people with tremors or limited dexterity. Targets that pass only through spacing are easy to miss.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers target size.

plainEnglish.summary: The default human language of each page can be programmatically determined. (In HTML, W3C's sufficient technique is the lang attribute on the html element; techniques are informative.)
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A correct but generic code, such as en with no region, can't tell a screen reader which accent or spelling conventions to use.

plainEnglish.summary: The human language of each passage or phrase can be programmatically determined. Exempt: proper names, technical terms, words of indeterminate language, and words or phrases that have become part of the surrounding language.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Proper names and technical terms are exempt, so a page full of untagged foreign names can still be mispronounced.

plainEnglish.summary: When any component receives focus, that doesn't start a change of context. WCAG defines a change of context as a change of user agent, viewport, focus, or content that changes the meaning of the page.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Focus-triggered changes that fall short of a "change of context", such as large panels expanding, can still disorient people using magnification.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft forbids a change of context on focus; the related ones cover notification and focus movement.

plainEnglish.summary: Changing the setting of a component doesn't automatically cause a change of context, unless the user was told about this behavior before using the component.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Advance notice that is technically present, such as a sentence above the form, is easily missed. Keyboard users browsing a select with arrow keys can trigger navigation by accident.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft forbids a change of context on input.

plainEnglish.summary: If pages in a set repeat any of these help mechanisms, they appear in the same order relative to other page content, unless the user changes it: human contact details, a human contact mechanism, a self-help option, or a fully automated contact mechanism.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Consistently placed help can still be unhelpful, such as a chatbot that can't reach a person.

plainEnglish.summary: If an input error is automatically detected, the item in error is identified and the error is described to the user in text.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An error summary that names fields but is not linked to them makes screen reader users hunt back through the form to find each problem.

plainEnglish.summary: Labels or instructions are provided when content requires user input. WCAG defines a label as text, or a component with a text alternative, presented to the user to identify a component.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Placeholder-only labels disappear as soon as people type, so users with memory or attention difficulties lose track of what a field wants, and prefilled fields can't be checked.

plainEnglish.summary: Information the user has already entered, or that was provided to them, and that must be entered again in the same process, is either auto-populated or available to select. Exceptions: re-entry is essential, is needed for security, or the earlier information is no longer valid.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Offering the earlier value in a hard-to-find control satisfies "available to select" but still makes people re-enter data.

plainEnglish.summary: No step of an authentication process requires a cognitive function test, unless that step offers one of: another method that doesn't rely on one; a mechanism to help complete it; a test that is recognizing objects; or a test that is identifying non-text content the user provided. WCAG defines a cognitive function test as remembering, manipulating or transcribing information, such as remembering a password, transcribing characters, correct spelling, calculations or puzzles. Name, email and phone number don't count.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Object-recognition CAPTCHAs are allowed at AA but are still very hard for many blind and low-vision users and people with cognitive disabilities.

plainEnglish.summary: For all interface components (including form elements, links and scripted components), the name and role can be programmatically determined; states, properties and values the user can set can be programmatically set; and changes to them are notified to user agents, including assistive technologies.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Custom widgets can expose a valid name and role yet not match expected keyboard behavior or announce in a useful order.

plainEnglish.summary: In content built with markup languages, status messages can be programmatically determined through role or properties, so assistive technologies can present them without them receiving focus. WCAG defines a status message as a change in content that isn't a change of context and that tells the user about success or results, waiting, progress, or errors.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Over-announcing (live regions for every update) can drown out the messages that matter.

plainEnglish.summary: Prerecorded audio in synchronized media has sign language interpretation.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A small or low-resolution interpreter window makes hand shapes and facial expressions hard to read.

plainEnglish.summary: Where pauses in the foreground audio are too short for audio description to convey the sense of the video, extended audio description is provided: the video pauses so there is time for more description. Applies to prerecorded video in synchronized media.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Frequent pauses can make the experience choppy if the description is longer than it needs to be.

plainEnglish.summary: All prerecorded synchronized media and all prerecorded video-only media have an alternative for time-based media: a document with correctly sequenced text descriptions of the visual and auditory information, and a way to achieve the outcome of any interaction.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A complete alternative is little use if users can't find it.

plainEnglish.summary: Text and images of text have a contrast ratio of at least 7:1, and large-scale text at least 4.5:1, with the same exceptions as 1.4.3.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Some readers find very high contrast uncomfortable, so a single fixed palette can't suit everyone.

wcag3Mapping.note: The draft's contrast measure is still to be determined.

plainEnglish.summary: For prerecorded audio-only content that is mainly foreground speech (not an audio CAPTCHA, audio logo, or singing or rapping), one of these is true: there are no background sounds, they can be turned off, or they are at least 20 decibels quieter than the speech, apart from occasional sounds of one or two seconds.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Even background music at 20dB lower can make speech hard to follow for people with hearing loss.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers background audio levels.

plainEnglish.summary: For blocks of text, a mechanism is available to: choose foreground and background colors; limit width to 80 characters (40 for CJK); avoid justified text; get line spacing of at least 1.5 and paragraph spacing at least 1.5 times the line spacing; and resize text to 200 percent without horizontal scrolling in a full-screen window.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Relying on users to find browser settings means many never benefit.

plainEnglish.summary: Images of text are used only for pure decoration, or where a particular presentation of text is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: None beyond 1.4.5. This removes 1.4.5's customization exception.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft restricts images of text.

plainEnglish.summary: All functionality can be operated through a keyboard interface without needing specific timing for individual keystrokes. Unlike 2.1.1, there is no exception for path-dependent input.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Keyboard alternatives for drawing or gesture tools can be technically present but tedious.

plainEnglish.summary: Timing is not an essential part of the event or activity, except for non-interactive synchronized media and real-time events.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Removing time limits can conflict with security policies, which need a design answer rather than an exception.

plainEnglish.summary: The user can postpone or suppress interruptions, except interruptions involving an emergency.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Notification settings buried in account preferences are rarely discovered.

plainEnglish.summary: Nothing on the page flashes more than three times in any one second. Unlike 2.3.1, there is no threshold exception for small or dim flashes.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: None beyond 2.3.1.

plainEnglish.summary: Information about the user's location within a set of pages is available.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Breadcrumbs that only reflect the URL structure may not match how users think about the site.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers location within a set of pages.

plainEnglish.summary: A mechanism is available so that the purpose of each link can be identified from the link text alone, except where the purpose would be ambiguous to everyone.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Visually hidden text added to make links unique can mismatch what speech-input users see and say.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers link purpose.

plainEnglish.summary: Section headings are used to organize the content.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Headings used for styling rather than structure create a misleading outline.

plainEnglish.summary: Pointer targets are at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels. Exceptions: an equivalent target of that size is on the same page; the target is in a sentence or block of text; the browser sets the size and the author hasn't changed it; or the presentation is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: None beyond 2.5.8. This is the stricter version.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers target size.

plainEnglish.summary: A mechanism is available for identifying specific definitions of words or phrases used in an unusual or restricted way, including idioms and jargon.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A glossary on a separate page technically counts but interrupts reading.

plainEnglish.summary: A mechanism is available for identifying the expanded form or meaning of abbreviations.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The abbr title attribute alone isn't reliably exposed to keyboard, touch or screen reader users.

plainEnglish.summary: When text needs reading ability above lower secondary education level (after removing proper names and titles), supplemental content or a simpler version is available.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Readability formulas measure sentence and word length, not whether people actually understand the text.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft uses a reading-level test.

plainEnglish.summary: Changes of context happen only at the user's request, or there's a mechanism to turn such changes off.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Opening new windows or tabs without warning remains common and disorienting.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft restricts changes of context to user request.

plainEnglish.summary: Context-sensitive help is available: help text related to the function currently being performed. A general help page doesn't meet the definition.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Help that is technically context-sensitive but terse can still leave users stuck.

plainEnglish.summary: For pages that require the user to submit information, at least one is true: submissions are reversible; input is checked and the user can correct it; or the user can review, confirm and correct before final submission.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: None beyond 3.3.4. This extends it to every submission.

plainEnglish.summary: Live audio-only content, such as a live audio stream, has an alternative that presents equivalent information.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A text summary posted afterwards doesn't help people following the event live.

plainEnglish.summary: In content built with markup languages, the purpose of user interface components, icons and regions can be programmatically determined.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Tools that personalize interfaces for people with cognitive disabilities depend on semantics that most sites don't yet provide.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft requires identifying the purpose of components, icons and regions.

plainEnglish.summary: When an authenticated session expires, the user can continue the activity without losing data after signing in again.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Re-authentication that drops the user on a home page technically keeps their data but loses their place.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers re-authentication.

plainEnglish.summary: Users are warned how long they can be inactive before data is lost, unless the data is kept for more than 20 hours of inactivity.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A warning shown once at the start of a long form is forgotten by the time it matters.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers warnings about inactivity timeouts.

plainEnglish.summary: Motion animation triggered by interaction can be disabled, unless the animation is essential to the functionality or the information conveyed.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A site-level toggle that users must find before they feel ill doesn't help on first visit.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft is specific to animation triggered by interaction.

plainEnglish.summary: There is more than one way to find a page within a set of pages, except pages that are the result of, or a step in, a process.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Two ways that both depend on a complex mega-menu don't really give users a choice.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft requires more than one way to find a page.

plainEnglish.summary: When a component receives keyboard focus, no part of it is hidden by content the author created.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: None beyond 2.4.11. This is the full version.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers focus being obscured.

plainEnglish.summary: When the focus indicator is visible, an area of it is at least as large as a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter of the unfocused component, and has a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states. It doesn't apply if the browser sets the indicator and the author can't adjust it, or if the author hasn't modified the indicator or its background.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: An indicator can meet the area and contrast numbers yet be hard to spot if it is inside the component or similar to other states such as hover.

wcag3Mapping.note: The draft says "sufficient" without giving numbers.

plainEnglish.summary: Functionality that uses multipoint gestures (such as pinch) or path-based gestures (such as a swipe pattern) can also be operated with a single pointer without a path-based gesture, unless the gesture is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A single-pointer alternative hidden in a menu technically passes but is rarely discovered.

plainEnglish.summary: For single-pointer functionality, at least one is true: nothing happens on the down-event; the function completes on the up-event and can be aborted before or undone after; the up-event reverses whatever the down-event did; or completing on the down-event is essential.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Undo that is only available briefly in a toast is easy to miss for screen reader and magnifier users.

plainEnglish.summary: Functionality operated by device motion (such as shaking or tilting) or user motion can also be operated through interface components, and responding to motion can be turned off. Exceptions: the motion works through an accessibility-supported interface, or it's essential and doing it another way would invalidate the activity.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A motion setting that is off only once the user finds it means people with tremors may trigger actions by accident on first use.

plainEnglish.summary: Content doesn't restrict the input methods available on a platform, except where that is essential, needed for security, or needed to respect user settings.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Switching off touch on "desktop" layouts strands people who use a touchscreen with a keyboard.

plainEnglish.summary: A mechanism is available for identifying the pronunciation of words whose meaning, in context, is ambiguous without knowing how they're pronounced.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: This rarely comes up in English but matters in languages like Japanese and Hebrew.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft covers pronunciation.

plainEnglish.summary: Navigation that is repeated on multiple pages within a set of pages appears in the same relative order each time, unless the user changes it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: The same order in a different place on the screen still makes users hunt for it.

plainEnglish.summary: Components with the same functionality within a set of pages are identified consistently.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Consistent labels with inconsistent icons, or the reverse, still undermine recognition.

wcag3Mapping.note: No provision in the current draft requires consistent identification of all same-function components.

plainEnglish.summary: If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correcting it are known, the suggestions are provided, unless that would compromise the security or purpose of the content.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Correct suggestions can still be hard to act on, for example when they appear only in a summary at the top of a long form.

plainEnglish.summary: For pages that create legal commitments or financial transactions, modify or delete user-controllable data, or submit test responses, at least one is true: submissions are reversible; input is checked for errors and the user can correct them; or the user can review, confirm and correct before final submission.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: A review step that users can click through without noticing errors technically confirms, but doesn't prevent costly mistakes.

plainEnglish.summary: No step of an authentication process requires a cognitive function test, unless that step offers another method that doesn't rely on one, or a mechanism to help complete it. Unlike 3.3.8, there are no object-recognition or personal-content exceptions.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: None beyond 3.3.8. This removes 3.3.8's object-recognition and personal-content exceptions.

plainEnglish.summary: Nothing. WCAG 2.2 marks this criterion obsolete and removed, so it can't be failed under 2.2. WCAG 2.2's introduction notes that organizations required by policy to conform to WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 may still need to test and report it.
plainEnglish.whyItMatters: Invalid markup that doesn't affect the accessibility tree isn't a WCAG failure, but it can make behavior inconsistent across browsers and assistive technologies.

wcag3Mapping.note: Obsolete and removed in WCAG 2.2.
